segments.voice: Yesterday, air is the guru: the first gift every life receives, so a duty to keep clean. The smoke has cleared. Now the second line of that same verse.
screen: `AIR IS THE GURU.` → `NOW, THE NEXT LINE.`

segments.voice: A hot afternoon in the strip of dirt behind Arjan's building. Bebe has come over with a tray of chili seedlings for Arjan's mom, and she's watering the bed with the hose running full blast, telling stories, paying no attention to the puddle. Mrs. Haddad walks out, says hello, and quietly turns the tap down. Bebe raises an eyebrow. Mrs. Haddad smiles: my book says every living thing was made from water. Bebe, never one to lose a quote-off, answers: my Guru says water comes first. Simran sets down her phone. This could go either way.
screen: `A HOSE RUNNING FULL BLAST.` → `MRS. HADDAD TURNS IT DOWN.` → `MY BOOK SAYS. MY GURU SAYS.` → `THIS COULD GO EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Underneath the quote-off is an old question: is water just a utility, or is it sacred? Bebe's line is from Guru Nanak, in Asa di Var on Ang 472. In paraphrase: first, water is life, by which everything is made green. And the Japji's closing lines, on Ang 8, name water the father. A father is someone who provides, someone you come from, someone whose gift you don't pour on the ground. So the Sikh answer is family: you don't waste your father's water. Mrs. Haddad's line is from the Qur'an, surah twenty-one, verse thirty. In paraphrase: God made every living thing of water, and asks, will they not then believe? Shared ground, and it's real: two grandmothers, two books, one thirst. Both see water as the beginning of life, not something to take for granted. And one honest difference. In the Qur'an, water's life-giving power is a sign, pointing the reader toward the Creator. In the Japji, water sits inside a family picture, a father, beside a Guru and a mother. A sign, and a father. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: in the Japji's picture, air, water and earth are Guru, father and mother, and day and night are the two nurses in whose lap the whole world plays. Bebe looks at the puddle. Then she reaches over and turns the hose off completely. Mrs. Haddad offers her a cutting of mint.
screen: `A UTILITY, OR SACRED?` · `FIRST, WATER IS LIFE.` · `QUR'AN: EVERY LIVING THING OF WATER.` · `A SIGN, AND A FATHER.` · then, large: `WATER IS THE FATHER.`

segments.voice: Fill a glass slowly from a tap, or pour water from one cup into another, and listen to it the whole time. When it's full, stop, and drink a little slowly. Whatever you don't drink, give to a plant instead of the sink.
Water is the father. From the Japji's last lines: water as the one who provides, whose gift you don't waste, because everything green begins with it.
